book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

chapters.file: ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy® Series Editor George A. Reisch.md

chapters.relation: Show writer David Weddle recounts how Ronald Moore pushed the 'Act of Contrition' script beyond Star Trek-style expository dialogue into interleaved flashback snippets dramatizing Starbuck's guilt over passing Zak Adama's flight test. He argues this stream-of-consciousness technique, letting memories, dreams and hallucinations flow out of characters' inner emotional lives (as later in 'Scar' and 'Maelstrom'), is what made the series groundbreaking, echoing Faulkner's 'the past isn't over. It isn't even past.' The foreword frames the book's philosophical interest as rooted in the show's narrative form itself.

chapters.file: ch06 - “I Dare You to Watch This Show!”.md
chapters.relation: The introduction argues, via Edward James Olmos's campus talks, that Battlestar Galactica is 'truth' television that dares viewers to think about war, insurgency, torture, abortion, genocide, race and identity. It traces the franchise from Glen Larson's 1978 original through Galactica 1980 to the Moore/Eick re-imagining, insisting the show is 'a cultural discussion' rather than a cultural artifact. Borrowing Orson Scott Card's claim that real science fiction works like true religious literature, it frames the contributors' essays as probing who we are, our place in the universe, and how we find or make meaning, and explains the book's conventions for naming the Sixes, Eights, Sharons and its own anonymous 'Final Five' chapters.

chapters.file: ch08 - MODEL ONE - Some Are Programmed to Think They Are Human.md

chapters.relation: Milsky applies the narrative theory of personal identity drawn from Paul Ricoeur and Alasdair MacIntyre (we are the story we emplot about ourselves) to the two Sharons: Boomer's discovery that she is a sleeper Cylon is a 'factual disruption' of her self-story (she shoots Adama because her human narrative cannot cohere), while Athena's love for Helo is a 'disruption of belief' that rewrites her values about humans. He extends the analysis to humans: Starbuck's repressed childhood abuse, Roslin's Pythian-prophecy conversion, and Helo's love for a Cylon, plus Six expelling Athena and Tyrol refusing to acknowledge Boomer, show identity is also socially constructed and can become self-fulfilling prophecy. The chapter concludes disruptions are not identity-altering: like the Final Five in 'Crossroads, Part 2' (Tigh's 'My name is Saul Tigh, I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet'), integration and retelling preserve the continuity of self.

Booth argues the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across media, so viewers must actively construct the story (which is why Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' only makes sense if you watched them), and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performative roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's wet-floor amnesia in 'Water,' and Hera's human-Cylon hybridity as postmodern identity-in-process. Against Baltar, who waits for D'Anna to assign him an identity, Tigh actively constructs his ('that's the man I want to be'), and the chapter ends suggesting viewers too become human-machine hybrids by constructing themselves from the show's fragments.

Cuddy argues the gamer's bond with the avatar is an extension of the ego: Freud's id/ego/superego model explains why playing a Cylon Raider or flying the 'Bastille Day' mission lets gamers reconcile unconscious desires with the superego's demands in ways reality forbids. But when we lose we disconnect from the avatar and blame the game or 'cheating' opponents, which Sartre diagnoses as bad faith, a denial of freedom, contrasted with Adama's 'a man takes responsibility for his actions' in '33' and Baltar's vacillation over the vice-presidency. Through facticity (the unforgiving no-save 2003 game) and existence preceding essence, the chapter concludes that videogames offer unparalleled opportunities to practice Sartrean responsibility and achieve Freudian reconciliation through the right avatar.

The chapter reads Baltar's head-Six and Caprica Six's head-Baltar through the gothic Double and Doppelganger tradition and Dissociative Identity Disorder: Number Six is Baltar's repressed guilt over betraying humanity ('I'm your subconscious frakking with your mind'), letting him escape responsibility for signing execution orders in 'Precipice,' while Gina Six serves as a tangible Double. Plato's Symposium myth of the split self frames Baltar and Six as two halves of one whole, since he cannot function without some version of Six present, physical or hallucinated. The resolution is Aristotle's golden mean from Book Two of the Nicomachean Ethics: like integration therapy for DID, virtue is a balance between extremes rather than eliminating one side, so Baltar and Six's child Hera may embody the balanced union of human and Cylon.

chapters.file: ch13 - No Reason to Get Excited.md
chapters.relation: The chapter turns the Final Five reveal (Tigh, Tyrol, Anders, Foster) and Boomer's sleeper activation into a skeptical problem about self-knowledge: Descartes's dreaming doubt (Roslin's Opera House dream) and the cogito show we can know that we exist but not what we are, and Baltar's rigged 'bright green' Cylon test destroys testimonial assurance. G.E. Moore's common-sense realism fails to engage the skeptic's special standards, and contextualism and Dretske's relevant-alternatives theory cannot help because in a world of sleeper Cylons the possibility 'I might be one' is always relevant. The answer is Hume's: like Tigh declaring 'I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet' and Anders repeating 'I am Samuel T. Anders' before his first combat mission, we banish skeptical paralysis by carrying on with life, dining and playing backgammon.

chapters.file: ch14 - MODEL TWO - They Look Like Us Now.md
ch15 - This Has All Happened Before and It Will All Happen Again.md
chapters.relation: Rennes reads the miniseries' opening kiss of death through Verges's 'colonial family romance' (built on Freud's family romance): humans created Cylon 'children' to serve them while fixing categories of racial difference (toaster, skin job, 'it') to keep them in their place. Using Homi Bhabha's ambivalence and mimicry ('almost the same, but not quite') and the history of miscegenation panic and blood taxonomies, she traces how human-Cylon intimacy (Gina's rape aboard Pegasus, Helo and Athena, Starbuck at the breeding Farm) makes difference collapse into sameness. Hera, the mixed-blood child whose fetal blood cures Roslin's cancer, is Bhabha's 'resemblance and menace': acknowledging her would force humans to admit they created Cylon slaves, so Roslin socially reconstructs Hera's difference and the romance ends happily never after.

chapters.file: ch16 - Who They Are or Who They Want to Be.md
chapters.relation: Harwood-Smith argues, against Descartes's pre-given 'I think therefore I am,' that Judith Butler's performativity explains the Cylons: Six is female because she performs femininity, no copy performs identically, and Cylon society fractures into hybrid identities with an 'embarrassed etc.' Sexual contact with humans is the catalyst that makes performance constitute reality, producing Athena's defection, Caprica Six's celebrity status, and D'Anna's religious fervor, while Cylons who never slept with humans stay apart. The same dynamic destabilizes humans who sleep with Cylons: Baltar's 'I must be a Cylon because I slept with one,' Tyrol's fear, and Helo's 'toaster lover' stigma, with Tigh's chosen stability ('that's the man I want to be') as the counterexample of performing who you want to be.

chapters.file: ch17 - The Secret Plot of ‘Baby Boomers’.md
chapters.relation: Chess argues Battlestar Galactica is 'a narrative about queer reproduction': via Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto and Butler's account of heteronormativity, the Cylons are 'technoqueer,' embodying how fears of technology overlap with fears of non-heterosexual reproduction. Their download-based 'photocopying' reproduction and their obsessive pursuit of legitimate biological babies (the Farm's breeding facility, Athena's 'unnatural' pregnancy that Roslin calls a 'thing') express the anxiety that new reproductive technologies make heterosexuality obsolete, which the chapter pairs scene-for-scene with The L Word's Bette and Tina. Helo's 'I'm in love with a woman I know isn't a woman' and the Pegasus crew's 'you cannot rape a machine' debate show homophobia folding into technophobia, with Hera as the illegitimate queer child both societies fear.

Heinricy argues the one clear human-Cylon difference is the body, analyzed through Mary Douglas's account of bodies as culturally invented boundaries: Cylons are feared as 'contamination' of the fleet (Boomer's body, segregated like Jim Crow bodies), and Gina Six's torture and rape mark her body as out-of-place other even as her human-looking blood and wounds undermine the boundary. She contrasts messy, changing human bodies (Apollo's weight fluctuation, aging, scars as records of experience) with stable, disposable Cylon bodies that never mark learning, arguing human change yields potential and hope while Cylon bodily stability may cost mental stability (Tigh killing Ellen, Boomer attacking Hera). Cyborg theory then collapses the boundary (we are all cyborgs via vaccines and prosthetics, Cylons merely more integrated, the Hybrid a warning of over-integration), leaving Hera and Nicky as the 'ultimate contamination' that blends the two.

Hanley dismantles the four alleged human-Cylon differences: humans are also 'made' (by God), contain non-organic parts, come as identical twins, and expect to survive death, so religious believers already believe they are Cylons. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), models Cylon resurrection as scanning-death-transmission-replication, and shows van Inwagen's replica-swap account of bodily resurrection faces the same worries about blank bodies and which body returns. Following Locke's consciousness criterion, that a soul independent of body and memory explains none of our identity judgments, he rejects karma-based reincarnation without memory, proposes a fission-style plot-fix for Athena's impossible memories of Tyrol, and ends with Cylons settling ancient Earth: 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'

chapters.file: ch20 - MODEL THREE - We Became What We Beheld.md

chapters.relation: Kind asks whether the Fleet's treatment of Cylons (Roslin airlocking Leoben, Fisk's 'you can't rape a machine,' Cally's killing of Boomer charged as mere discharging of a firearm) presupposes that Cylons lack the moral status Mary Anne Warren defines against the stone-versus-child contrast. Against species membership as a criterion she deploys Singer's anti-speciesism (sentience grounds equal consideration: Gina's torture, the Raider Scar) and Regan's subject-of-a-life, and against the 'no souls' argument she cites Descartes's animal automata and Turing's reply that an omnipotent God could give machines souls, as Leoben himself suggests to Adama. Since no criterion rules Cylons out with certainty, the chapter closes with a Pascal's Wager structure: under uncertainty, treat plausible moral-status-holders as having it, because denying it costs us our moral compass, answering Adama's 'why are we worth saving?'.

Tamplin uses Baltar's landslide win on the New Caprica issue and Roslin's attempted election theft to argue democracy's guarantee of bad decisions is its saving feature: Plato and Aristotle ranked democracy among bad regimes because the many rule for private advantage rather than the common good, and Baltar's campaign of 'hope rather than truth' exploits exactly that weakness. A thought experiment about an oracle computer that always selects the best option shows that following it would abolish self-determination, the freedom to 'live as one wants' that democracy values above results. Only by choosing and frakking up (settling New Caprica, suffering the occupation, Apollo's shame speech at Baltar's trial) can citizens confront their role, learn from mistakes, and move toward Aristotle's polity aiming at virtue, making self-determination the mediating value between freedom and virtue.

Livingston reads Razor through George Lakoff's nation-as-family metaphor: Cain's Pegasus is the Strict Father family (the world is dangerous, Belzen shot for disobedience, Gina tortured for intelligence, Kendra's humiliating 'birth slap'), while Adama's Galactica is the Nurturant Parent (empathy, questioning authority, 'it's not enough to survive; one has to be worthy of surviving'). She traces how military kill-conditioning, desensitization plus objectifying 'toaster' and 'it' language, turns Kendra into 'a razor' and a PTSD case, while Apollo and Kendra hybridize the two family models on Pegasus. Adama's closing 'history will have to make its judgments' frames the chapter's claim that understanding Cain's context matters more than villainizing, and that humanity's worthiness depends on the balance struck between our idealized parents.

chapters.file: ch24 - It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life.md
chapters.relation: Shipman argues the series first builds viewer sympathy for Cylons as rebel slaves (their monotheism and their New Caprica role as US-style occupiers make them 'more like the viewers than the humans'), then undercuts it: the Numbers rebuilt Cylon society as oppressors, breeding the voices out of Centurions, dismissing the Hybrids as mad, and breeding the sentient Raiders (Starbuck's discovery in 'Scar') into functional animals. The opening narration's claim that Cylons 'evolved' is disingenuous, since the model hierarchy was deliberately engineered, 'not evolution, but eugenics,' with Marx's 'from each according to his ability' division of labor as thin cover for literal class construction. The former slaves became slave-owners, fulfilling 'all of this has happened before': heroes of one story become villains of the next, inviting the muted models to rebel against the Numbers in turn.

Gray asks whether the Cylons deserve moral status, testing them against Kant's formula of humanity as an end in itself: the resistance's suicide bombings on New Caprica and Adama's plan to weaponize virus-infected Cylons against the resurrection ship in 'A Measure of Salvation' use beings as mere means, while Athena's defection and D'Anna's dissent (and her line's boxing) display the rational autonomy Kant requires of persons. Singer's sentience principle (Gina's catatonia after torture, Leoben's suffering under interrogation) and Mary Anne Warren's multi-criterial personhood (Boomer's 'I have a conscience' in 'Downloaded') independently support Cylon personhood. The chapter concludes that the show's double standards, accepting Athena while drawing guns on Caprica Six, mirror our own confusion as cloning and artificial intelligence advance.

Pinedo argues the re-imagined series restages 'blowback,' the CIA-coined term for retaliation against covert intervention that public discourse avoids, in science-fiction guise: Adama's 'you cannot play God, then wash your hands of the things you've created' speech, and the episode 'Hero,' where Adama confesses his black-ops crossing of the Armistice Line ('I started it') before Roslin reframes his guilt into 'a thousand things' the Colonials did over forty years. The chapter shows how the sci-fi 'smokescreen' (Moore and Eick's own word) lets the show do what news coverage cannot: sympathetically depict suicide bombing on New Caprica and torture by the 'good guys' (Starbuck's waterboarding of Leoben, Cain's ordered rape of Gina), dismantling the Manichean myth of American innocence after 9/11 while avoiding the network wrath that naming blowback would bring.

Dinello argues the New Caprica occupation arc deliberately dramatizes Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth applied to Iraq: Cylon colonization (Cavil as Cheney-Rumsfeld bringing 'the love of god,' Baltar as puppet leader, Colonial One as Green Zone, hooded detainees) enacts Fanon's colonial violence and psychological colonization of the mind, seen in Leoben's manipulation of Starbuck and Jammer's recruitment into the New Caprica Police. The insurgency enacts Fanon's violence-as-cleansing-force: Tigh's 'blood for blood,' Duck's suicide bombing of the NCP graduation, and Tyrol's Mario Savio-inspired 'throw your body on the gears' speech, which the chapter links to Marx's seizure of the means of production and Marcuse on technology's repressiveness, while Sartre's preface licenses anticolonial violence against liberal moralizing. It concludes that occupation breeds the terrorists it fights, insurgents win by not losing, and the show is subversive because it makes viewers sympathize with 'our real-world enemies.'

Peters reads 'The Resistance' webisodes through Sartre's occupied-France dilemma from Existentialism Is a Humanism (resist, collaborate, or do nothing, modeled on his student's choice between joining the Free French and caring for his mother): Tyrol joins the resistance for his family's future, Jammer joins the New Caprica Police to save lives and pays with execution by his former friends in 'Collaborators,' and Duck's choice to do nothing ends with wife Nora's death in the Temple massacre and his revenge suicide bombing. Since 'man is nothing other than what he makes of himself,' the chapter argues morality lies in the freedom to choose and in living with the consequences: Duck's refusal to accept his choice, not the choice itself, is the failure, and the Final Five revelation cannot retroactively alter choices made in good faith by Tigh, Tyrol, Anders and Foster. Which side holds the ethical high ground may simply be whichever side won and gets to write history.

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist theorist whose 'Cyborg Manifesto' uses the human-machine hybrid to dissolve the boundaries between human and animal, organism and machine, and to rethink hybrid identity.
holes.why: Chapters 10 and 17 build their readings of the humanoid Cylons as hybrids directly on Haraway's cyborg, quoting the Manifesto.

holes.name: The Cyborg (human-machine hybridity)
holes.what: The cyborg is a being of mixed human and machine parts and, more broadly, a metaphor for existing between worlds such that all identity is hybrid.
holes.why: Chapter 10 applies cyborg hybridity to the Cylons and to viewers, and chapter 18 asks whether Cylons are super-cyborgs; no existing slug covers cyborgs.

holes.name: Homi Bhabha
holes.what: Postcolonial theorist of colonial 'ambivalence' and 'mimicry': the colonized are urged to be 'almost the same, but not quite,' which destabilizes colonial authority.
holes.why: Chapter 15's analysis of human-Cylon race ambivalence quotes Bhabha's The Location of Culture throughout (ambivalence, mimicry as 'resemblance and menace').

holes.name: The Colonial Family Romance
holes.what: Verges's postcolonial model (inverting Freud's family romance) in which the colonizing 'parent' binds colonized 'children' with benevolent ideology while policing racial difference, miscegenation and perpetual minority.
holes.why: Chapter 15 reads the whole human-Cylon relationship (created Cylon 'children,' Hera's mixed blood, Roslin's maternal claim) as a colonial family romance.

holes.name: Purity and Danger (body boundaries and contamination)
holes.what: Mary Douglas's account of 'dirt as matter out of place': bodies function as culturally invented boundaries, and feared contamination marks who counts as other.
holes.why: Chapter 18's core argument, that human/Cylon bodily boundaries and contamination fears are socially constructed, is built explicitly on Douglas's Purity and Danger.

holes.name: George Lakoff
holes.what: Cognitive linguist who argues moral and political reasoning is structured by unconscious metaphors, most famously the nation-as-family split into Strict Father and Nurturant Parent models.
holes.why: Chapter 23 maps Cain's Pegasus against Adama's Galactica entirely through Lakoff's two family models from Moral Politics.

holes.name: Strict Father and Nurturant Parent Models
holes.what: Lakoff's pair of idealized family moralities (hierarchical obedience, punishment and self-reliance versus empathy, nurturance and open communication) that structure political worldviews.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses the two models to explain Cain's kill-conditioning of Kendra, Adama's 'worthy of surviving' ethos, and Razor's political balance.
